introduction: The readings begin with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the harm done by fault-finding and on keeping written language moderate and courteous; the letters that follow, written for Bahá’í communities, affirm a believer's right and duty to put criticism before the elected Assembly while warning against airing it elsewhere or making a habit of challenge. Proverbs, the Gospels, the Qur’an and Franklin say much the same about the tongue. Because the guide sets limits on criticism, it is read here also with those who prized it: Nathan before David, Socrates the gadfly, Paul withstanding Peter, and Milton, Mill and Jefferson on free discussion.
questions: Where do the readings draw the line between criticism that is a duty and criticism that is forbidden?
Mill says an opinion not fearlessly discussed becomes a dead dogma. How might a community keep discussion alive within the limits described here?
Nathan rebuked a king and Paul withstood Peter to the face. What would the readings say of each?
What do the readings ask of the one who is criticized?

outside.why: Proverbs likens a word fitly spoken to apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Jesus tells the accusers that whoever is without sin among them may cast the first stone.
Pope's advice to critics is that good nature and good sense must ever join: to err is human, to forgive divine.
The Qur’an forbids spying and backbiting, and likens it to eating the flesh of a dead brother.
Proverbs observes that a soft answer turns away wrath, but grievous words stir up anger.
Paul's rule for speech among believers is speaking the truth in love.
The Preacher advises against cursing the king even in thought, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice.
Nathan tells King David to his face, Thou art the man. Is there a censure of rulers that faith itself requires?
Proverbs holds that faithful are the wounds of a friend, while the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Socrates calls himself a gadfly given to the state by God, to stir a great and tardy steed into life.
Roosevelt gives the credit to the man in the arena, who errs and comes short again and again, for there is no effort without error.
Jesus asks that a fault be told first between thee and him alone.
Mill holds that an opinion not fully, frequently and fearlessly discussed becomes a dead dogma. What is lost when disagreement may be voiced only to those with authority to act on it?
Paul asks believers at law with one another why they do not rather take wrong.

Jefferson would let dissenters stand undisturbed, as monuments of the safety with which error may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it. Does a community lose more by a critic's excess or by guarding against it?
Franklin made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction of others and all positive assertion of his own view.
Paul says he withstood Peter to the face, because he was to be blamed. When is an open challenge to a leader loyalty, and when is it undermining?
Proverbs says that iron sharpens iron, and so a man sharpens the countenance of his friend.
Leviticus joins the two duties: rebuke thy neighbour, bear no grudge, and love him as thyself.
Milton would let truth and falsehood grapple in a free and open encounter. Is the study of principles an answer to dissatisfaction, or a preparation for voicing it well?
Peter asks how often he must forgive, and is told until seventy times seven.
James tells believers not to speak evil one of another, for whoever judges his brother judges the law.
The Dhammapada says a sage should notice not the misdeeds of others but his own.

ephesians-speaking-the-truth-in-love.text: But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ

ephesians-good-to-the-use-of-edifying.text: Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers

galatians-withstood-him-to-the-face.text: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed

proverbs-he-that-rebuketh-a-man.text: He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue

jefferson-error-of-opinion.text: If there be any among us who would wish to dissolve this Union or to change its republican form, let them stand undisturbed as monuments of the safety with which error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it
jefferson-error-of-opinion.author: Thomas Jefferson
